nodes.name: Discrete analytic function
nodes.statement:
A function $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is said to
be {\em discrete analytic}
 if
\[ \forall (x,y)\in \mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad
\dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}=\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}.\]

nodes.name: Pointwise powers of z are not all discrete analytic
nodes.statement:
For example, the functions $z:=x+iy$ and $z^2$
are discrete analytic in the sense of Definition \ref{maindef},
but $z^3$ is not.

nodes.statement_short: $z$ and $z^2$ are discrete analytic but $z^3$ is not, so pointwise products fail.

nodes.name: Describing discrete analytic polynomials and rational functions
nodes.statement:
Thus a natural question arises, how to describe
all complex polynomials in two variables $x,y$ whose restriction
to the integer grid $\mathbb{Z}^2$ is discrete analytic, and, more
generally, rational discrete analytic functions.

nodes.name: Falling factorial $x^{[n]}$
nodes.statement:
In what follows, $\Omega$ stands for one of two sets: $\mathbb{Z}$ or
$\mathbb{Z}_+$, and $x^{[n]}$ denotes the polynomial of degree $n$
defined by
\[ x^{[n]}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(x-j)\] (if $n=0,$
$x^{[0]}:=1$).

nodes.name: Generating function of falling factorials
nodes.statement:

\[
(1+t)^x=\sum_{k=0}^x x^{[k]}\frac{t^k}{k!},
\]

in section \ref{sec5}.

space of functions $f:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$  is defined by
$$(\delta f)(x)=f(x+1)-f(x),\quad x\in\Omega.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement:
To show the uniqueness of $\hat f(n)$, assume that \eqref{tay} holds
 for some function $\hat f(n)$
and apply  the identity
\[ \delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}\]
repeatedly to obtain \eqref{fou1}.\\

Next, let the function $\hat f(n)$ be defined by \eqref{fou1}.
Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay1}, the series
$$\tilde f(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$
converges absolutely for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and defines a function
$\tilde f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}.$ Hence \eqref{fou1} holds with
$\tilde f$ replacing $f$ and
$$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$
 Now one can verify that
\[ \forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad
(\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)
\]
by induction on $x$: If
$$ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)$$
then

\begin{multline*}
\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad
(\delta^nf)(x+1)=(\delta^nf)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}f)(x)\\=
(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}\tilde f)(x) =(\delta^n\tilde
f)(x+1).\end{multline*} It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to
obtain \eqref{tay}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by repeated difference identity; existence by induction on $x$ showing all differences of $f$ and the series agree.

$$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$

nodes.name: Induction on x

\[ \forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad

\]

nodes.statement_short: Induction on $x$ shows $\delta^n f=\delta^n\tilde f$ everywhere.

It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to
obtain \eqref{tay}.

nodes.name: Fourier transform on $\mathbb{Z}_+$
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then the function $\hat
f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},$ defined by \eqref{fou1}, is said to be
the Fourier transform of $f$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Polynomial on $\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement:
Suppose  that a function $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is such that
$$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x)=p(x),$$
where $p(x)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then such
a polynomial $p(x)$ is unique, and we shall call the function $f$
itself a polynomial. If $f(x)\not\equiv 0,$ the degree of $f(x)$
is the same as the degree of $p(x)$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: A function on $\mathbb{Z}$ agreeing with a complex polynomial is called a polynomial, with that polynomial's degree.

nodes.name: Fourier transform of a polynomial has finite support
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f
:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of the
restriction $f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}$. Then the function $\hat f$ has a
finite support and
$$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement:
Note that
$$\deg(\delta f)=\deg(f)-1$$
(if $f=\mathrm{const},$ $\delta f=0$). Hence
$$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow \delta^nf=0.$$
Since $$(\delta f)_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}=\delta(f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}),$$
\eqref{fou1} implies that
$$\forall n>\deg(f),\qquad \hat f(n)=0.$$
It follows that
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial,
which coincides with the polynomial $f(x)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ and hence on
$\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Differences lower the degree, so high Fourier coefficients vanish; the finite series is a polynomial agreeing on $\mathbb{Z}_+$.

nodes.name: Coefficients vanish above degree
nodes.statement:
Note that
$$\deg(\delta f)=\deg(f)-1$$
(if $f=\mathrm{const},$ $\delta f=0$). Hence
$$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow \delta^nf=0.$$
Since $$(\delta f)_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}=\delta(f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}),$$
\eqref{fou1} implies that
$$\forall n>\deg(f),\qquad \hat f(n)=0.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Degree drops under $\delta$, so $\hat f(n)=0$ for $n>\deg f$.

nodes.name: Polynomial identity
nodes.statement:
It follows that
$$\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial,
which coincides with the polynomial $f(x)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ and hence on
$\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: The finite series is a polynomial agreeing with $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, hence on $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement:
By Proposition
\ref{p01},
$$ f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]},$$ where
$\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is a function with finite
support.
 Consider the
polynomial

nodes.name: Rational function on $\mathbb{Z}_+$
nodes.statement:
A function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is said
to be {\em rational} if there exist polynomials
$p,q:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\forall x\in \mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad q(x)\not=0,$$
and
$$\forall x\in \mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}.$$

nodes.label: defrat1

nodes.name: Realization of rational functions on $\mathbb{Z}_+$
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be given. Then $f(x)$ is a
rational function if and only if there exist a polynomial $p(x)$
and matrices $A,B,C$ such that
\[ \sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset,
\]
 and
\begin{equation} f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.8
nodes.statement:
We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a
complex variable can always be written in the form
\[
r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B,
\]
where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at
infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes.
Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite)
poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1,
MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and
thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.\\

Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if
and only if it is the restriction on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ of a rational
function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, that is
if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the
matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Recall the state-space realization of matrix rational functions and restrict to $\mathbb{Z}_+$ with no poles there.

nodes.name: Recall realization theorem
nodes.statement:
We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a
complex variable can always be written in the form
\[
r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B,
\]
where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at
infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes.
Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite)
poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1,
MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and
thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Recall that rational functions have minimal realizations whose poles are the spectrum of $A$.

nodes.name: Apply to $\mathbb{Z}_+$
nodes.statement:
Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if
and only if it is the restriction on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ of a rational
function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, that is
if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the
matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Rational on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ means restriction of a rational function with no poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$.

nodes.name: Growth bound for Fourier transform of rational functions
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be rational, and let $\hat
{f}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of $f$.
Then
$$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\leq 1.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
assumptions:
let $\hat
{f}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of $f$
also_stated_at:
The purpose of this section is to prove (see Theorem \ref{lim1}
below) that any rational function $f\,\,:\,\,\mathbb
Z_+\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathbb C$ (see Definition
\ref{defrat1}) has a unique representation
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \widehat{f}(n)x^{[n]},
\]
where
\[
\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(n!|\widehat{f}(n)|\right)^{\frac{1}{n}}\le
1.
\]
nodes.label: lim1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.9
nodes.statement:
According to Proposition \ref{ABC}, there exist a polynomial
$p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that
$\sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset$ and
$$f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B.$$ Hence, for $n>\deg(p)$,
$$|\hat{f}(n)n!|=|(\delta^nf)(0)|\leq\|C\|\cdot\|B\|\cdot\|A^{-1}\|\cdot
\prod_{j=1}^n\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|.$$ Since
$$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|=1,$$
$$\forall\epsilon>0,\,\,\exists M,N\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\forall
n\in\mathbb{Z}_+\quad:\quad n\geq N\Longrightarrow|\hat{f}(n)n!|\leq
M(1+\epsilon)^n,$$ and the conclusion follows.

nodes.statement:
The linear {\em difference operators} $\delta_x,\delta_y$ on the
space of functions $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$
are defined by
$$(\delta_xf)(x,y):=f(x+1,y)-f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yf)(x,y):=f(x,y+1)-f(x,y).$$

\[ (\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)=

\]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement:
First, fix $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and consider the function
$f_x:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad
y\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a
unique function $\hat{ f_x}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\forall y\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$
the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by
$$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$
Next, fix $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and  consider the function
$g_n:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ given by
$$g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ By the same Proposition
\ref{tay2}, there is a unique function
$\hat{g_n}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that
$$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad g_n(x)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]};$$
the function $\hat{g_n}(m)$ is given by
$$\hat{g_n}(m)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(0,0)}{m!n!},\quad m\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$
Thus
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2,\qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)
\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ It remains to set $\hat
f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m).$

$f_x:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad

$$\forall y\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$
the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by
$$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$

nodes.name: Polynomials vanishing on $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement:
Let $p(z,w)$ be a complex polynomial in two
variables. Then, $p\big|_{\mathbb{Z}^2}=0$ if and only if $p\equiv 0$.

variables

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement:
Write
\[
p(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^N p_n(z)w^n,
\]
where the $p_n$ are polynomials in $z$. The equations
$p(z,w)\equiv 0$ for $w=0,1,\ldots N$ lead to (using a
Vandermonde determinant) that $p_0(z),p_1(z),\ldots, p_N(z)$
vanish on $\mathbb{Z}$ and hence identically.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Expand in powers of $w$ and use a Vandermonde determinant.

nodes.name: Polynomial on $\mathbb{Z}^2$
nodes.statement:
Suppose  that a function $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is such that
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad f(x,y)=p(x,y),$$
where $p(x,y)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then in
view of Theorem \ref{tautology}, such a polynomial $p(x,y)$ is
unique, and we shall call the function $f$ itself a polynomial. If
$f(x,y)\not\equiv 0,$ the degree of $f(x,y)$ is the same as the
degree of $p(x,y)$.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: A function on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ agreeing with a (unique) complex polynomial is called a polynomial.

nodes.name: Two-variable Fourier transform of a polynomial
nodes.statement:
Let $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f

restriction $f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+^2}}$. Then the function $\hat f$ has a
finite support and
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$

nodes.statement:

$$\forall (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2,\,\,\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,

f)(x,y)=0,$$ the function $\hat f$ has a finite support.  It
follows that
$$\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial,
which coincides with the polynomial $f(x,y)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+^2$ and
hence on $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

nodes.name: Discrete Cauchy-Riemann operator characterization
nodes.statement:
A function $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is
discrete analytic if and only if
$$\forall (x,y)\in \Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\qquad(\bar{\mathcal{D}} f)(x,y)=0,$$
where
\[ \bar{\mathcal{D}}:=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y.\]

conclusions:
A function $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is
discrete analytic if and only if
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is discrete analytic iff $\bar{\mathcal D}f=0$ with $\bar{\mathcal D}=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y$.

In particular, $q(x,y)\equiv 0$ if and only if $p(x)\equiv 0$. If
this is not the case,
$$\deg(q)=\deg(p).$$

nodes.name: Vanishing on the axis forces vanishing
nodes.statement:
Let $q:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a discrete analytic polynomial,
such that $q(x,0)\equiv 0.$ Then $q(x,y)\equiv 0.$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
Assume the opposite, then $\deg(q)>0,$ and $q$ can be chosen so
that $\deg q$ is the smallest possible. Observe that
$(\delta_xq)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, that $
(\delta_xq)(x,0)\equiv 0,$ and that $\deg(\delta_xp)<\deg(p).$
Hence $(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv 0.$ Since $q(x,y)$ is discrete
analytic, Definition \ref{maindef2} implies that
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\delta_yq)(x,y)=
\dfrac{i-1}{2}((1-i+\delta_y)\delta_xq)(x,y)= 0.$$ Thus
$$(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_yq)(x,y)\equiv 0$$
and hence $q=\mathrm{const}$ - a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement:
The uniqueness of the polynomial $q(x,y)$ follows from Lemma
\ref{l1}. The existence in the case $p=\mathrm{const}$ is clear: it
suffices to set
$$q(x,y)=p(0).$$  If $p\not=\mathrm{const}$ we proceed by induction on
$d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$
is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the
induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial
$f(x,y)$,  such that
 $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$
 and  $\deg(f)=d-1.$ Let $g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be defined by
 $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$
 then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial,
 $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$
\begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad
(\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\=
i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))=
(\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*}
 Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a
 polynomial $h:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that
 $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv
 g(x,y).$$
 Since
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\bar D
h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the
polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic. Finally, since
$$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$
$h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set
$$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement:
The analyticity is clear because $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ and we have
$$e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^n c_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\mathbb{D}.$$
where
$$c_n(x,y)=\dfrac{d^n}{dz^n}e_{x,y}\Bigm|_{z=0}.$$
Since
$$e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^{n+1}
c_{n}(x,y)}{n!},$$
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad
(\delta_xc_{n})(x,y)=nc_{n-1}(x,y)$$ (if $n=0,$ $c_0(x,y)\equiv 1$
and $(\delta_xc_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$). Similarly, since
\[
\begin{split}
\dfrac{e_{x+1,y+1}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)}{1+ i}-\dfrac{e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y+1}(z)}{1-i}&=\\
&\hspace{-5cm}=\left(
(1+z)\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}-1\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1+i}-\left(
1+z-\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1-i}\\
&\hspace{-5cm}=0,
\end{split}
\]
we have
$$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad
(\bar Dc_{n})(x,y)=0.$$ Thus, for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, the function
$c_n:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is discrete analytic. Next, we show
by induction that
\[ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y).
\]
Indeed, for $n=0$,
$$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$
Assume that, for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$,
$$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$
then, in view of \eqref{hu3},
$$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv
(n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence
$$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$
But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete
analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and
$$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$
It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\mathrm{const};$$ since
$$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$
one concludes that
$$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$
and \eqref{hu4} follows.

nodes.name: Origin of the name Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement:
We now explain the name given to this product. Recall that the
classical Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem concerns uniqueness of
solutions of certain partial differential equations with given
initial conditions. See for instance \cite{MR93j:26013}. In
Clifford analysis, where the pointwise product of hyperholomorphic
functions need not be hyperholomorphic, this theorem was used by
F. Sommen in \cite{MR618518} (see also \cite{bds}) to define the
product of hyperholomorphic quaternionic-valued functions in
$\mathbb R^4$ by extending the pointwise product from an
hyperplane. In the present setting of expandable functions the
discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with
prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis also
has a unique solution. This is why the pointwise product on the
horizontal positive axis can be extended to a unique expandable
function, which we call the C-K product.
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement_short: Named after the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem, as in Sommen's product for hyperholomorphic functions extending from a hyperplane.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8.4
nodes.statement:
In $(iii)$, we denote by $e^{itA}$ the unitary one-parameter
group generated by the self-adjoint operator $A$ from $(i)$. The
matrix representation of $A$ with respect to the ONB
$e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ is:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
 & & &   &   & & & &\\
 & & &  & 0  & & & &\\
 & & &n-2&n-1&0& & &\\
 & & &n-1&n-1&n&0& &\\
 & & &    &n &\boxed{n}&n+1&\\
 &  & &   &0 &n+1&n+1&n+2\\
 &   & &   &0&0&n+2&n+2\\
 &    & &   & & &0&\\
 \end{pmatrix}
\]
It is therefore a banded infinite matrix with terms going to
infinity linearly with $n$. It follows from \cite{MR507913} that
$A$ is essentially self-adjoint.\\

$(ii)$ By definition of $\mathcal{Z}$ and $\delta_x$
\[
\begin{split}
[A,\delta_x^*](e_n)&=(A\delta_x^*-\delta_x^*A)(e_n)\\
&=\frac{1}{2}(e_n+e_{n+1}+e_{n+2})\\
                   &=\frac{1}{2}(I+\delta_x^*+\delta_x^{*2})e_n,
\end{split}
\]
and hence the result.\\

$(iii)$ We have
\begin{equation} e^{itA}be^{-itA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty
\frac{(it)^n}{n!}\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n (b),
\end{equation}
and
\[ \left({\rm ad}~A\right)^{n+1} (b)=[A,\left({\rm
ad}~A\right)^n b],
\]
We verify \eqref{sum} on monomials of $\delta_x$ and $\delta_x^*$
using \eqref{wert} and induction. See \cite{MR671318,MR548006}
for more details regarding limits.

nodes.name: Schur class $\mathscr S$
nodes.statement:
To set these results in a wider setting, let us recall a few
facts on Schur analysis, that is, on the study of functions
analytic and contractive in the open unit disk. If $s_0$ is such a
function (in the sequel, we write $s_0\in\mathscr S$), the
operator of multiplication by $s_0$ is a contraction from the
Hardy space of the open unit disk $\mathbf H_2$ into itself.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Schur analysis studies analytic contractive functions in the disk; their class is $\mathscr S$, whose elements act as contractive multipliers on $\mathbf H_2$.

nodes.name: $\lozenge$-inverse of $I-zA$

satisfies
\[
(I_{\mathcal{H}}-zA){\lozenge} (I_{\mathcal{H}}-zA)^{-{\lozenge}}=I_{\mathcal{H}},
\]
and it is the only function in $T\mathcal{O}$ with this property.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.3
nodes.statement:
Assume first that $s\in\mathcal{O}$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier
on $\mathbf{H}$. Then $s=s\lozenge1\in\mathbf{H}$ and hence $s=Ts_0$ for some
$s_0\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Furthermore, let $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Since
$s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$,  $s_0f\in\mathbf{H}_2.$ Since
$$\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_{\mathbf{H}}\geq\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_{\mathbf{H}}=\|T(s_0f)\|_{\mathbf{H}}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2},$$
$s_0\in\mathscr{S}.$

Conversely, if $s=Ts_0$ where $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$, and $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$ then
$s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$ and
$$\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_{\mathbf{H}}=\|T(s_0f)\|_{\mathbf{H}}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}
\leq\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_{\mathbf{H}}.$$
Thus $s$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$.

nodes.statement_short: Both directions via the unitary $T$, which intertwines $\lozenge$-multiplication with pointwise multiplication.

nodes.name: Properties of $\partial$ on $\mathbf{H}$
nodes.statement:
The operator $\partial$ is bounded on $\mathbf{H}$; moreover,

$$\partial^*\partial=I_{\mathbf{H}}-C^*C,\quad \partial\partial^*=I_{\mathbf{H}},$$
where $Cf:=f(0)$. Furthermore, the reproducing kernel of $\mathbf{H}$ is
given by
$$K_{\mathbf{H}}(z,w)=Ce^{z\partial}e^{w^*\partial^*}C^*.$$
